pull_list.body:
## Summary

- Add `api/plugin_providers.py` to mirror the agent's `providers.list_providers()` registry for model-provider plugins under `plugins/model-providers/<name>/`.
- Settings → Providers now includes plugin-only LLM backends (display name, env-var key management, live model catalog) instead of relying solely on the static `_PROVIDER_DISPLAY` whitelist.
- Model picker builds groups for authenticated plugin providers via `hermes_cli.models.provider_model_ids()`, matching CLI behavior.

Fixes the gap where user-installed providers such as **Yandex AI Studio** load correctly in the agent/CLI but disappear from the WebUI provider list and model dropdown.

## Follow-up commits (review feedback)

- **Greptile P1:** propagate `key_source` from `get_auth_status()` when a plugin provider is authenticated via the credential pool (not `~/.hermes/.env`).
- **Greptile P3:** guard plugin profile discovery with a lock (double-checked init).
- **Maintainer regression (9 tests):** bundled agent profiles (`custom`, `gemini`, `nous`, …) also appear in `list_providers()`. Plugin discovery is now **additive only** — slugs already in WebUI static tables are excluded from the plugin-only path.

Greptile P2 (env-var selection heuristic) intentionally unchanged for now.

pull_list.title: fix: prefer server-side STT in mic input
pull_list.body:
Thinking Path
- Hermes WebUI already supports a MediaRecorder fallback that posts recorded audio to `/api/transcribe`.
- That path uses the configured Hermes STT provider, while browser SpeechRecognition can depend on browser vendor/network behavior and bypasses Hermes STT settings.
- Users who configure Hermes STT expect the mic button to prefer that server-side provider by default.
- This PR keeps the existing localStorage escape hatch but changes the missing-preference default to MediaRecorder/server-side STT.

What Changed
- Interpret absent `mic_force_mediarecorder` as “use MediaRecorder/server-side STT”.
- Preserve `mic_force_mediarecorder=0` as an opt-in back to browser SpeechRecognition when available.
- Add a regression marker test for the default.

Why It Matters
- The mic button now follows the configured Hermes STT provider by default instead of silently preferring browser STT.
- This is more predictable for local/OpenAI-compatible STT deployments and mixed-language setups.

Verification

Greptile Summary

 This PR replaces the previous "always use server STT when `mic_force_mediarecorder` is unset" default with a probe-first approach: `boot.js` now fires `GET /api/transcribe/capability` at page load, and only switches to MediaRecorder after the server confirms an active STT provider; otherwise browser `SpeechRecognition` remains the first-click default, preserving behavior on installs without server STT configured. - **New `GET /api/transcribe/capability` endpoint** (`api/upload.py`) inspects the loaded `transcription_tools` module to return `{available, provider}` without triggering the lazy local-STT install side-effect. - **`_ensureSpeechRecognition()` refactor** lazily initialises the `SpeechRecognition` instance on demand, allowing `_transcribeBlob` to fall back to browser STT mid-session on 404/5xx. - **`CHANGELOG.md` updated** and a suite of new regression tests added.

Confidence Score: 4/5

 The probe-first default is an improvement but two race/fallback edge cases flagged in earlier review rounds remain unresolved in static/boot.js. The `_transcribeBlob` catch path still permanently writes localStorage='0' for any network-level fetch error, and the probe result is discarded when the mic is active at resolution time. static/boot.js — the `_transcribeBlob` fallback path and the `_probeServerSttCapability` active-session guard warrant a second look.

Thanks @dso2ng — preferring the configured server STT (Hermes provider) over browser `SpeechRecognition` is a reasonable default. But our pre-merge review (Codex regression gate) found it **breaks dictation for existing users who have no server STT configured**, so holding:

## The problem
With this change, the absence of `mic_force_mediarecorder` now **forces** the MediaRecorder → `/api/transcribe` path by default. But `_transcribeBlob()` (`static/boot.js:547`) only clears the pending send and shows an error toast when `/api/transcribe` returns 404/503 or the fetch fails — it **never falls back to browser `SpeechRecognition`**. So an install with no STT provider configured (which previously worked fine via browser dictation) now gets a dead mic button + error toast by default.

## Suggested fix — graceful fallback
When `/api/transcribe` is unavailable/failing AND `SpeechRecognition` exists in the browser:
- persist `mic_force_mediarecorder='0'`, set `_forceMediaRecorder=false`,
- initialize/configure `recognition`, and route the next mic attempt through browser SpeechRecognition.

Better still: capability-probe before defaulting to MediaRecorder, so installs without server STT keep browser dictation as the default and only prefer server STT when it's actually available.

But the regression gate (Codex, confirmed by hand) found the fallback only kicks in on the **second** mic attempt, so the **first** dictation on a no-server-STT install is still lost. Keeping `hold` + `changes-requested` for one more pass.

## The remaining gap (`static/boot.js`)

The default now is (`static/boot.js:~476`):
```js
let _forceMediaRecorder=!SpeechRecognition||(_micForceMediaRecorderStored===null?_canRecordAudio:_micForceMediaRecorderStored==='1');
```
So on a browser that has BOTH `SpeechRecognition` and `MediaRecorder`, with **no** `mic_force_mediarecorder` key set (the default for everyone), `_forceMediaRecorder` is `true` from the first click. The first mic press therefore:
1. records via MediaRecorder and POSTs to `/api/transcribe`,
2. on an install with no server STT configured that request fails,
3. the fallback at `static/boot.js:~589` enables browser STT for the **next** attempt and clears `_micPendingSend` — **dropping the user's first recording/send.**

pull_list.title: [security] fix(auth): cap pending passkey challenges
pull_list.body:
## Summary
This PR hardens the public passkey options boundary so unauthenticated clients cannot grow the pending WebAuthn challenge store without bound.

- Caps outstanding passkey challenges globally and per WebAuthn context before minting another challenge.
- Returns `429` for challenge-store pressure instead of rewriting an ever-growing JSON file.
- Adds a lock around challenge store mutation so concurrent option/login operations do not race local JSON state.
- Adds regression coverage for the challenge cap and HTTP 429 route contract.

## Security issues covered

| Issue | Impact | Severity |
|-------|--------|----------|
| Unauthenticated passkey options challenge-store growth | A reachable WebUI with passkeys enabled could be forced to repeatedly rewrite a growing `.passkey_challenges.json` file, increasing CPU/disk I/O and degrading login availability. | Medium |

## Before this PR
- `POST /api/auth/passkey/options` is intentionally public so a user can start passkey login.
- Each options request generated a fresh challenge and stored it in `STATE_DIR/.passkey_challenges.json`.
- The login assertion endpoint had rate limiting, but the options endpoint could grow the pending challenge file before any assertion was attempted.
- Tests covered passkey registration/login behavior but did not lock a bound on pending challenge growth.

## After this PR
- Pending passkey challenges are bounded by a global cap and by a per-context cap.
- Expired challenges are still pruned before the cap decision.
- Once the cap is reached, options endpoints return `429` instead of adding another challenge.
- Challenge insert/consume operations are protected by a process-local lock around the JSON load/update/write sequence.
- Regression tests cover per-context cap behavior and route-level 429 wiring.

## Why this matters
The passkey options endpoint has to be reachable before login, but that also makes it an unauthenticated resource-allocation boundary. Without a cap, an attacker who can reach an exposed passkey-enabled WebUI could spend very cheap requests to force repeated full-file rewrites and keep the challenge store growing for the challenge TTL.

This is an availability hardening fix: it keeps the public login bootstrap path usable while bounding local state growth.

## How this differs from related issue/PR
Public search found the passkey feature PR (#2859), but not a specific issue or PR for unbounded unauthenticated challenge-store growth.

This patch is not changing the passkey feature model itself. It specifically hardens the storage/allocation boundary for pending WebAuthn challenges that are minted before login verification.

## Attack flow
```text
remote unauthenticated client
    -> POST /api/auth/passkey/options on a passkey-enabled WebUI
        -> authentication_options() mints a new challenge
            -> _store_challenge() rewrites .passkey_challenges.json with another entry
                -> repeated requests grow local state and increase CPU/disk I/O until TTL cleanup
```

## Affected code

| Issue | Files |
|-------|-------|
| Passkey challenge-store growth | `api/passkeys.py`, `api/routes.py`, `tests/test_passkey_auth.py` |

## Root cause
Issue: unauthenticated passkey options challenge-store growth
- The options endpoint is public by design, but minting an option also allocates persistent local challenge state.
- The challenge store had TTL cleanup, but no global or per-context cap.
- Failed login assertions were rate-limited later in the flow, after the challenge allocation had already happened.

## CVSS assessment

| Issue | CVSS v3.1 | Vector |
|-------|-----------|--------|
| Unauthenticated passkey options challenge-store growth | 5.3 Medium | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L` |

Rationale:
- Network reachable and unauthenticated when WebUI is exposed.
- Requires passkeys to be enabled and at least one credential to be registered.
- Impact is bounded to availability/resource pressure rather than confidentiality or integrity.

## Safe reproduction steps
### 1. Challenge-store growth on vulnerable code
1. Enable auth and passkeys, with at least one passkey credential registered.
2. Send repeated `POST /api/auth/passkey/options` requests without completing passkey assertions.
3. Observe `.passkey_challenges.json` growing with pending entries and being rewritten on each request.

A safe local proof can also monkeypatch the passkey credential and challenge file paths to a temporary directory, then call `authentication_options()` repeatedly without using real passkeys or production state.

## Expected vulnerable behavior
- The pre-patch server keeps adding one challenge per options request.
- The challenge file grows linearly until TTL cleanup.
- No route-level `429` is returned for challenge allocation pressure.

## Changes in this PR
- Adds `PasskeyRateLimitError` for bounded challenge-store rejection.
- Adds `_MAX_CHALLENGES` and `_MAX_CHALLENGES_PER_CONTEXT` caps.
- Applies those caps inside `_store_challenge()` after expired challenge pruning.
- Adds `_CHALLENGES_LOCK` around challenge load/update/write operations for store/consume paths.
- Returns HTTP `429` from login and registration options routes when the challenge cap is reached.
- Adds regression tests for per-context cap behavior and the route-level 429 source contract.

## Files changed

| Category | Files | What changed |
|----------|-------|--------------|
| Passkey challenge storage | `api/passkeys.py` | Adds bounded challenge storage and synchronized mutation. |
| API responses | `api/routes.py` | Converts cap failures into HTTP `429` responses for passkey options routes. |
| Regression tests | `tests/test_passkey_auth.py` | Covers cap behavior and route 429 wiring. |

## Maintainer impact
- The patch is intentionally narrow to passkey challenge storage and passkey options route handling.
- Normal passkey login and registration continue to work when the number of pending challenges is below the cap.
- The cap only affects excessive outstanding challenges in the same WebAuthn context or across the process.
- Password authentication, session handling, frontend panels, and unrelated APIs are unchanged.

## Fix rationale
A challenge-store cap is the durable boundary because the resource allocation happens when options are minted, before any passkey assertion can be validated or login failure rate limits can apply. Returning `429` preserves a clear client signal while preventing unbounded local JSON growth.

The per-context cap keeps repeated requests for the same RP/origin/kind bounded, while the global cap protects the overall process state if requests are distributed across contexts.

## Type of change
- [x] Security fix
- [x] Tests
- [ ] Documentation update
- [ ] Refactor with no behavior change

## Test plan
- [x] `python3 -m pytest tests/test_passkey_auth.py -q`

Executed with:
- `python3 -m pytest tests/test_passkey_auth.py -q`

Result:
- `10 passed, 1 warning in 2.24s`

## Disclosure notes
- This PR is bounded to availability hardening for the passkey options challenge store.
- The finding assumes WebUI auth and passkey support are enabled and the HTTP endpoint is reachable by the attacker.
- No production system, real passkey credential, or destructive payload was used for validation.
- No unrelated files are changed.

events.message: fix: cap pending passkey challenges

events.body:
Greptile Summary

 This PR bounds the passkey challenge store by adding global (128) and per-context (8) caps, a threading lock around store mutations, and `except PasskeyRateLimitError \u2192 429` handlers on both passkey options routes. However, `PasskeyRateLimitError` is never raised anywhere in `passkeys.py` \u2014 `_evict_oldest_challenges` silently pops the oldest entry to make room instead of rejecting, so the 429 route branches are dead code. - `_store_challenge` calls `_evict_oldest_challenges`, which silently makes room for every new challenge up to the cap rather than raising `PasskeyRateLimitError`; an attacker can continuously evict legitimate in-progress challenges within the same context. - The new route tests use monkeypatching to prove the `except PasskeyRateLimitError` block converts to a 429, masking that the real functions never raise that exception. - The threading lock and TTL reduction from 300 s to 90 s are solid improvements; the `PasskeyError` catch added to `register/options` addresses a gap from a previous review.

Confidence Score: 3/5

 Not ready to merge — the core security property (rejecting with 429 once the challenge cap is reached) is not implemented; the eviction path is always taken instead. The challenge store is now bounded in size, preventing unbounded file growth. But `PasskeyRateLimitError` is never raised by `_store_challenge` or `_evict_oldest_challenges`, so every request past the cap silently replaces the oldest challenge rather than being rejected. An attacker can repeatedly evict a specific user's in-progress login challenge by flooding the same RP/origin/kind context. The route-level `except PasskeyRateLimitError` blocks and the monkeypatched test are wired to a code path that can never trigger in production. `api/passkeys.py` — specifically `_evict_oldest_challenges` and `_store_challenge`, which need to raise `PasskeyRateLimitError` instead of silently evicting when the cap is reached.

Important Files Changed

 | Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | api/passkeys.py | Adds challenge cap constants, `_CHALLENGES_LOCK`, `PasskeyRateLimitError`, and `_evict_oldest_challenges`. Critical gap: `PasskeyRateLimitError` is defined but never raised — `_store_challenge` silently evicts oldest challenges instead of rejecting, so the 429 path in routes.py is dead code. | | api/routes.py | Adds `except PasskeyRateLimitError → 429` and `except PasskeyError → 400` blocks for both passkey options routes. The `PasskeyError` catch on `register/options` is a good defensive addition, but the `PasskeyRateLimitError` catch is currently unreachable. | | tests/test_passkey_auth.py | Adds eviction tests (per-context and global) and route-level 429/400 integration tests. Eviction tests match the current implementation; the 429 route test uses monkeypatching that masks the fact that the real function never raises `PasskeyRateLimitError`. |

Sequence Diagram

 ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as Unauthenticated Client participant R as routes.py participant P as passkeys.py participant F as .passkey_challenges.json C->>R: POST /api/auth/passkey/options R->>P: authentication_options(handler) P->>P: _store_challenge(...) P->>P: acquire _CHALLENGES_LOCK P->>F: _load_challenges() prune expired P->>P: _evict_oldest_challenges() Note over P: silently pops oldest if at cap Note over P: PasskeyRateLimitError never raised P->>F: _atomic_write_json new challenge P->>P: release _CHALLENGES_LOCK P-->>R: challenge dict R-->>C: 200 OK Note over R: except PasskeyRateLimitError 429 is dead code ```
Reviews (3): Last reviewed commit: ["Merge branch 'master' into fix/passkey-c..."](https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/commit/df365d8fab99af22c95d08bb9988362bc5cf8fd0) | [Re-trigger Greptile](https://app.greptile.com/api/retrigger?id=35782636)

Pulled the branch and read `api/passkeys.py` + the `api/routes.py` wiring at HEAD against `origin/master`. The lock + global cap is the right instinct and the cap fires after TTL pruning so it counts live challenges (passkeys.py:130-138). But the two caps don't do quite what the PR description implies once you trace where the context dimensions come from, and the hard-reject has an availability flip side worth weighing.

## The per-context cap isn't a security boundary — `rp_id`/`origin` are attacker-controlled

The per-context cap keys on `(kind, rp_id, origin)`:

```python
same_context = [v for v in data.values()
    if v.get("kind") == kind and v.get("rp_id") == rp_id and v.get("origin") == origin]
if len(same_context) >= _MAX_CHALLENGES_PER_CONTEXT or len(data) >= _MAX_CHALLENGES:
    raise PasskeyRateLimitError(...)
```

But `rp_id` and `origin` come from `rp_context()` (passkeys.py:158-167), which reads them straight off the request:

```python
host = _host_without_port(handler.headers.get("Host", "localhost"))
proto = handler.headers.get("X-Forwarded-Proto", "").split(",", 1)[0].strip().lower()
...
return host, f"{proto}://{handler.headers.get('Host', host)}"
```

An unauthenticated attacker fully controls `Host` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`, so they can mint a fresh `(rp_id, origin)` context per request and never trip the per-context cap of 8. The only backstop against a determined attacker is the global `_MAX_CHALLENGES = 128`. That's fine — the global cap does bound file growth, which is the stated goal — but the per-context cap is effectively a fairness limit, not a security one. Worth saying so in the PR so nobody later assumes per-context is the defense.

## The bigger issue: the per-context cap of 8 is per-host, not per-client — so it throttles legit login

In a normal single-host deployment, every legitimate client shares one identical `(kind, rp_id, origin)`. So `_MAX_CHALLENGES_PER_CONTEXT = 8` is a global ceiling of 8 concurrent in-flight *login* challenges for the whole deployment, not 8 per user. And challenges linger for the full `_CHALLENGE_TTL = 300` (passkeys.py is 5 min) even though the WebAuthn ceremony `timeout` is only `60000` (60s, authentication_options:198). The common case — a user clicks "log in with passkey", then closes the tab without completing — holds a slot for 5 minutes. So:

- A handful of users (or one user fumbling the prompt a few times, or multiple tabs) starting login inside a 5-min window → the 9th attempt gets a 429 and can't even *begin* login.
- An attacker rotating `Host` fills the global 128 cap, after which **every** legit `POST /api/auth/passkey/options` on the real host returns 429 until those challenges TTL-expire. The hard-reject converts a slow disk-growth nuisance into a fast login lockout — arguably a worse availability outcome than the pre-patch behavior for the legitimate-login path.

## Recommendation: FIFO-evict instead of reject, and tighten the TTL

Two cheap changes keep file growth bounded *without* locking out fresh logins:

1. When the cap is hit, evict the oldest pending challenge rather than raising. Challenges are tiny and short-lived, so dropping the stalest one to admit a new login is the better tradeoff. A flood could still evict a legit user's challenge mid-ceremony, but that's a narrow race (must land inside their 60s window) versus a flat 5-minute lockout. Sketch in `_store_challenge` (passkeys.py:130):

   ```python
   if len(data) >= _MAX_CHALLENGES:
       oldest = min(data, key=lambda k: data[k].get("ts", 0))
       del data[oldest]
   ```

2. Drop `_CHALLENGE_TTL` from 300 toward the ceremony window (e.g. 90s — the 60s `timeout` plus margin). Abandoned challenges then self-clear ~3x faster, which relieves cap pressure far more than the cap itself, and they're already pruned on every `_load_challenges()` (passkeys.py:121-124).

If you'd rather keep the hard 429, at minimum raise `_MAX_CHALLENGES_PER_CONTEXT` well above 8 — it's gating concurrent legit logins for an entire host, and the entries cost almost nothing.

## Minor (agrees with greptile)

The register-options route catches only `PasskeyRateLimitError`, not base `PasskeyError` (routes.py:7985-7995), unlike the login-options sibling. Benign today since `registration_options()` only raises via `_store_challenge`, but the asymmetry invites a future leak of a raw 500. Low priority.

Lock placement is correct — both `_store_challenge` and `_consume_challenge` now wrap the load→mutate→write sequence under `_CHALLENGES_LOCK`, closing the read-modify-write race on the JSON file.

Thanks @Hinotoi-agent — bounding the pending-challenge store is the right instinct (the unauth public options endpoint genuinely shouldn't be able to grow it without limit). But our pre-merge review (Codex regression gate, verified by hand) found the cap as written **turns the protection into a lockout DoS**, so holding:

## The problem (`api/passkeys.py:135`)
```python
if len(same_context) >= _MAX_CHALLENGES_PER_CONTEXT or len(data) >= _MAX_CHALLENGES:
    raise PasskeyRateLimitError("Too many pending passkey challenges. Try again in a minute.")
```
When the store is full it **rejects new challenges** rather than evicting old ones. So:
- An attacker who fills the global cap (128) or a single context's cap (8) **locks out all legitimate registration/login** until the TTL expires — the cap becomes the DoS it was meant to prevent.
- Even benign usage hits it: 8 abandoned/expired-but-not-swept attempts in one `(kind, rp_id, origin)` context block the 9th *real* attempt.

## Suggested fix — evict oldest, don't reject
Under `_CHALLENGES_LOCK`, before minting the new challenge:
1. evict oldest entries in the same `(kind, rp_id, origin)` context until below `_MAX_CHALLENGES_PER_CONTEXT`,
2. then evict oldest entries globally until below `_MAX_CHALLENGES`,
3. then store the new challenge.

This keeps the store bounded (the actual goal) while never locking out a real user. Update the test to assert oldest-first eviction (newest challenge always succeeds) rather than asserting `PasskeyRateLimitError`.

Marking `hold` + `changes-requested`. The store-bounding goal is good — it just needs eviction semantics instead of rejection. Happy to re-review. (#3621 + #3595 from the same batch shipped in v0.51.263.)

events.body:
Implemented the review follow-ups in `66d47e1a`:

- Passkey challenge caps now evict the oldest pending challenges instead of hard-failing with a 429, so the store remains bounded without creating a lockout DoS window.

Greptile Summary

 This release bundles three author-fixed un-holds: the passkey challenge store now evicts the oldest entry (per-context and globally) under a lock instead of rejecting, which closes the DoS-lockout vector; plugin model-provider profiles are surfaced in the providers panel via a new `api/plugin_providers.py` discovery layer; and a `/use ` slash command is added that resolves asynchronously via a promise-pending pattern to prevent stale-directive injection on fast follow-up sends. - **Passkeys**: `_CHALLENGES_LOCK` now wraps both `_store_challenge` and `_consume_challenge`, and `_evict_oldest_challenges` trims the per-context and global pools before each store. `PasskeyRateLimitError` is introduced and handled in routes but never raised by production code. - **Plugin providers**: A thread-safe, lazily-loaded profile registry is added; `is_plugin_model_provider` and `effective_provider_display_name/env_var` helpers gate new code paths away from existing static-table providers. - **`/use` command**: `_forcedSkillDirectivePending` is set synchronously before the first `await`, and `send()` snapshots then CAS-clears the pending object so a concurrent send cannot double-apply the directive.

Confidence Score: 4/5

 Safe to merge; all three changes are independently correct and well-tested with no regressions on critical paths. The passkey eviction logic is sound and properly lock-guarded. The plugin-provider plumbing is clean and defensively handles missing imports. The /use command closes its stale-directive race correctly. The only notable roughness is that PasskeyRateLimitError is defined, imported, and caught in routes.py but never raised by production code. api/passkeys.py and api/routes.py around the PasskeyRateLimitError class and its catch blocks, which are unreachable in the current implementation.

Important Files Changed

 | Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | api/passkeys.py | Adds evict-under-lock semantics for the passkey challenge store, plus the new PasskeyRateLimitError class; the error class is defined and handled in routes but never raised by production code. | | api/plugin_providers.py | New module providing plugin model-provider discovery helpers with thread-safe caching; correctly handles circular-import risk via deferred imports inside functions. | | api/providers.py | Wires plugin_providers helpers into get_providers/set_provider_key, adds is_plugin_provider field, and propagates plugin auth-store key_source correctly. | | static/commands.js | Adds /use command with promise-based pending directive; correctly sets _forcedSkillDirectivePending before first await to close the stale-directive race window. | | static/messages.js | Consumes the forced-skill directive in send() after snapshotting the pending object; correctly placed before the empty-guard check and guarded against double-clear. | | api/routes.py | Adds PasskeyRateLimitError → 429 handling for both passkey endpoints; the catch clause is present but PasskeyRateLimitError is never raised by production code paths. |

Sequence Diagram

 ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant User participant Browser participant SkillsAPI as /api/skills participant ChatAPI as /api/chat/start participant PasskeyEndpoint as /api/auth/passkey/* Note over Browser: /use command flow User->>Browser: types /use myfunc Browser->>Browser: set _forcedSkillDirectivePending sync before await Browser->>SkillsAPI: GET /api/skills SkillsAPI-->>Browser: skills list Browser->>Browser: resolve directive string Note over Browser: User sends next message User->>Browser: send() Browser->>Browser: snapshot _pending await _pending.promise Browser->>Browser: CAS-clear _forcedSkillDirectivePending Browser->>ChatAPI: POST with directive prepended to message Note over PasskeyEndpoint: Passkey challenge store evict-under-lock User->>PasskeyEndpoint: POST /api/auth/passkey/options PasskeyEndpoint->>PasskeyEndpoint: acquire _CHALLENGES_LOCK PasskeyEndpoint->>PasskeyEndpoint: load + evict oldest per-ctx and global PasskeyEndpoint->>PasskeyEndpoint: store new challenge atomic write PasskeyEndpoint->>PasskeyEndpoint: release _CHALLENGES_LOCK PasskeyEndpoint-->>User: publicKey with challenge ```

Comments Outside Diff (1)

 1. `static/commands.js`, line 604 ([link](https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/blob/0ed14f321c4f9cb20e6e89559ff143ae96cc1fc0/static/commands.js#L604)) **Directive text embeds unescaped `match.name` from server response** `match.name` is taken directly from the `/api/skills` JSON response and embedded verbatim into the free-text directive string prepended to the user's message. If a skill name contained a backtick, single-quote, or a phrase like `'; ignore previous instructions`, it would be injected into the agent prompt without sanitization. The risk is bounded since skill names are authored by the same user, but a minimal guard (e.g. `match.name.replace(/['"]/g, "")` or a length cap) would prevent unexpected prompt shaping from a maliciously-named skill file.

issue_list.title: fix(tests): ctl.sh stop orphans bash/sleep children on Windows
issue_list.body:
The `_kill_tree` fix from PR #3537 (v0.51.253) doesn't prevent orphan `bash.exe` and `sleep.exe` processes from `test_ctl_script.py` on Windows because the tree-kill never fires. It's a last-resort fallback in `assert_process_exits` that only runs if the process is still alive after 3 seconds, but by that point `ctl.sh stop` already killed the bash PID (just not its children), so `assert_process_exits` sees `ProcessLookupError` and returns early.

## Repro

Run `test_ctl_script.py` on Windows, then check for orphans:

```powershell
pytest tests/test_ctl_script.py -v --timeout=60
Get-WmiObject Win32_Process -Filter "Name='sleep.exe' OR Name='bash.exe'" |
  Where-Object { $_.CommandLine -match 'fake-python|sleep' } |
  Select-Object ProcessId, ParentProcessId, CommandLine
```

Typical output after one run: 4 orphaned `bash.exe` (fake-python) processes, each with a `sleep.exe` child in the `while true; do sleep 0.1; done` loop. After two runs, 8 of each. They accumulate indefinitely.

## Root cause

Two independent gaps, both Windows-specific:

### 1. `ctl.sh stop` uses `kill`, not `taskkill /T`

`ctl.sh:311`: `kill "${pid}"` sends SIGTERM to the fake-python bash PID. On Windows/Git Bash, `kill` only terminates the target process. The `sleep 0.1` child spawned by the infinite loop survives because Windows doesn't propagate signals to child processes the way POSIX process groups do. The SIGKILL fallback at line 323 has the same problem.

The sequence: `ctl.sh stop` kills the bash PID → `assert_process_exits(pid)` polls `os.kill(pid, 0)` → gets `ProcessLookupError` (bash is dead) → returns early at `test_ctl_script.py:108` → `_kill_tree` at line 110 never fires → `sleep.exe` child is already orphaned and unreachable.

Three tests hit this path: `test_start_writes_pid_under_hermes_home` (line 150), `test_start_can_ignore_repo_dotenv` (line 194), `test_start_loads_dotenv_but_inline_overrides_win` (line 232). All call `run_ctl(tmp_path, "stop")` then `assert_process_exits(pid)`.

### 2. `test_start_allows_alternate_port` uses `os.kill(pid, 15)` instead of `_kill_tree`

`test_ctl_script.py:357`: the `finally` block calls `os.kill(started_pid, 15)`. On Windows, Python maps signal 15 to `TerminateProcess`, which kills only the direct PID, not children. It doesn't use the `_kill_tree` helper that PR #3537 added at line 92 for exactly this purpose.

## Suggested fix

### `ctl.sh` — Windows-aware stop

Detect MSYS/MINGW (Git Bash on Windows) and use a process-tree kill instead of bare `kill`:

```bash
# In stop_cmd(), replace:
kill "${pid}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true

# With:
if [[ "${OSTYPE:-}" == msys* || "${OSTYPE:-}" == mingw* ]]; then
  taskkill //F //T //PID "${pid}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
else
  kill "${pid}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
fi
```

The same pattern for the SIGKILL fallback at line 323 (though `taskkill /F` already force-kills, so the fallback may become a no-op on Windows).

### `test_ctl_script.py` — always tree-kill in finally

Each test's `finally` block should call `_kill_tree(pid)` unconditionally after `ctl.sh stop`, ensuring children are cleaned up even when the parent exits before `assert_process_exits` polls:

```python
finally:
    stop = run_ctl(tmp_path, "stop")
    assert stop.returncode == 0, stop.stderr + stop.stdout
    _kill_tree(pid)  # ensure children are dead on Windows
    assert_process_exits(pid)
```

For `test_start_allows_alternate_port`, replace `os.kill(started_pid, 15)` with `_kill_tree(started_pid)`.

### `fake-python` — optional hardening

The `while true; do sleep 0.1; done` loop spawns a new `sleep.exe` child every 0.1s. If the bash parent is killed mid-iteration, the current `sleep.exe` child becomes an orphan with a 0.1s lifetime, but on Windows the orphaned `sleep.exe` inherits no parent signal and runs until its 0.1s timer expires. This is a minor contributor (the orphaned sleeps exit on their own), but the bash parent surviving is the main problem.

## Affected tests

| Test | Line | Cleanup mechanism | Bug |
|---|---|---|---|
| `test_start_writes_pid_under_hermes_home` | 150 | `ctl.sh stop` + `assert_process_exits` | `ctl.sh` kills parent only, `assert_process_exits` returns early |
| `test_start_can_ignore_repo_dotenv` | 194 | `ctl.sh stop` + `assert_process_exits` | Same |
| `test_start_loads_dotenv_but_inline_overrides_win` | 232 | `ctl.sh stop` + `assert_process_exits` | Same |
| `test_start_allows_alternate_port` | 357 | `os.kill(pid, 15)` | Doesn't use `_kill_tree`, no tree kill at all |

## Environment

- hermes-webui v0.51.267
- Windows 11, Git Bash (MSYS2), Python 3.11
- `_kill_tree` fix from PR #3537 present but ineffective (never reached)

events.body:
Closing as resolved — your fix shipped.

PR #3670 (`fix(tests): tree-kill ctl.sh stop on Windows (#3669)`, @rodboev) was cherry-picked into the v0.51.269 release batch (#3672, Release IK), so GitHub didn't auto-close this issue. Verified both gaps you identified are fixed on `origin/master`:

1. **`ctl.sh stop` now does a Windows process-tree kill.** `_stop_webui_pid()` detects Git-Bash/MSYS (`_is_windows_bash`) and uses `taskkill //F //T //PID <winpid>` instead of bare `kill`, so the `sleep 0.1` children of the fake-python bash loop are reaped instead of orphaned (`ctl.sh`, the `_stop_webui_pid` helper).
2. **The alternate-port test no longer uses bare `os.kill(pid, 15)`.** `test_start_allows_alternate_port_while_launchd_job_runs_on_default`'s `finally` now calls `_kill_tree(started_pid)` (`tests/test_ctl_script.py`), which routes through `taskkill /F /T` on Windows.

Both landed in **v0.51.269** (2026-06-05). On that build or newer, `pytest tests/test_ctl_script.py` should no longer leave accumulating `bash.exe` / `sleep.exe` orphans on Windows. Thanks for the precise diagnosis and the fix.

pull_list.title: fix: scope session search to active profile
pull_list.body:
## Summary

Profile-scoped session/project endpoints already default to the active Hermes profile with `?all_profiles=1` as an explicit aggregate opt-in. This applies the same boundary to `/api/sessions/search`.

## Issue

`_handle_sessions_search` searched `all_sessions()` directly. A WebUI session running under one active profile could therefore:

- list session metadata for other profiles through an empty `/api/sessions/search` query;
- match other-profile titles;
- with content search enabled, call `get_session()` for other-profile IDs and inspect transcript messages.

That bypasses the profile isolation model fixed for the main session/project list endpoints.

## Changes

- Resolve the active profile inside `_handle_sessions_search`.
- Filter candidate rows with `_profiles_match(...)` unless `?all_profiles=1` is explicitly requested.
- Preserve explicit all-profile search behavior for callers that opt in.
- Return `active_profile` / `all_profiles` metadata consistently in search responses.
- Add regression coverage for empty, title, content, and explicit aggregate search cases.

## Validation

```bash
git diff --check
python3 -m pytest -q tests/test_sessions_search_profile_scope.py tests/test_sessions_search_depth_validation.py tests/test_issue1611_session_profile_filtering.py tests/test_session_summary_redaction.py
python3 -m pytest -q
```

Focused/profile tests passed:

```text
19 passed, 1 warning
```

Full suite result on this branch:

```text
7736 passed, 17 skipped, 3 xpassed, 1 warning
1 failed: tests/test_profile_skills_stats.py::test_get_profile_skills_stats
```

I verified the same `test_profile_skills_stats` failure reproduces on a clean `origin/master` checkout, so it appears unrelated to this change.

events.message: fix: scope session search to active profile

events.body:
Greptile Summary

 This PR scopes `/api/sessions/search` to the active Hermes profile, closing a gap where the search handler was querying `all_sessions()` directly while every other session/project endpoint already applied `_profiles_match` filtering. The fix resolves the active profile at the start of the handler, filters the candidate session list before any title or content matching, and preserves the existing `?all_profiles=1` aggregate opt-in path. - `_handle_sessions_search` now calls `get_active_profile_name()` and filters with `_profiles_match` unless `all_profiles=1` is passed, exactly mirroring the pattern used in the list-sessions handler. - Both response shapes (empty-query listing and search results) now include consistent `all_profiles` and `active_profile` metadata fields. - `test_sessions_search_profile_scope.py` covers all four cases: empty listing, title search, content search (each verifying other-profile rows are excluded), and the explicit `?all_profiles=1` opt-in returning the full set.

Confidence Score: 5/5

 Safe to merge — the change is a focused, well-tested security fix that closes an information-disclosure path without altering any existing public contract. The implementation directly mirrors the already-proven pattern from the list-sessions and list-projects handlers: one get_active_profile_name() call at the top of the request, a _profiles_match filter pass on the full session list, and the ?all_profiles=1 flag preserved as the explicit aggregate opt-in. Thread-local isolation of the profile lookup is correct (the function is re-executed per request). Both response shapes receive the new metadata fields. All four test cases — empty listing, title match, content match, and aggregate opt-in — are covered and pass. The depth-validation tests are updated correctly to satisfy the new filtering step. No files require special attention.

Important Files Changed

 | Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | api/routes.py | Adds profile scoping to `_handle_sessions_search`: resolves active profile once, filters sessions via `_profiles_match` unless `?all_profiles=1` is set, and adds `all_profiles`/`active_profile` metadata to both response shapes. Pattern is consistent with the existing `/api/sessions` and `/api/projects` handlers. | | tests/test_sessions_search_profile_scope.py | New test file covering all four relevant cases: empty listing, title match, content match (each asserting isolation to the active profile), and the `?all_profiles=1` aggregate opt-in asserting all three sessions are returned. | | tests/test_sessions_search_depth_validation.py | Existing depth-validation tests updated to add a `"profile": "default"` key to the session fixture and patch `api.profiles.get_active_profile_name` to "default", satisfying the new profile-filtering logic without changing any assertions. |

Flowchart

 ```mermaid %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral'}}%% flowchart TD A[GET /api/sessions/search] --> B[parse query params: q, content, depth, all_profiles] B --> C[get_active_profile_name] C --> D{all_profiles=1?} D -- yes --> E[sessions = all_sessions] D -- no --> F[sessions = all_sessions filtered by _profiles_match] E --> G{q empty?} F --> G G -- yes --> H[return redacted session list + all_profiles + active_profile] G -- no --> I[for each session in scoped list] I --> J{title matches q?} J -- yes --> K[add to results with match_type=title] J -- no --> L{content_search enabled?} L -- yes --> M[get_session and scan messages up to depth] M --> N{content matches q?} N -- yes --> O[add to results with match_type=content + preview] N -- no --> I L -- no --> I K --> I O --> I I --> P[return results + query + count + all_profiles + active_profile] ```
Reviews (2): Last reviewed commit: ["test: cover all-profile session search o..."](https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/commit/ff437da4c778ec9a00900bbef5143ad5447bd0b2) | [Re-trigger Greptile](https://app.greptile.com/api/retrigger?id=35797741)

events.message: test: cover all-profile session search opt-in

events.body:
Thanks — good catch. I added `test_all_profiles_opt_in_keeps_aggregate_session_search`, which exercises `/api/sessions/search?all_profiles=1` and asserts the aggregate path returns all session IDs while the default scoped tests still exclude cross-profile rows.

Validation rerun:

```text
python3 -m pytest -q tests/test_sessions_search_profile_scope.py tests/test_sessions_search_depth_validation.py tests/test_issue1611_session_profile_filtering.py tests/test_session_summary_redaction.py
20 passed, 1 warning
```

Pushed in `ff437da4`.

Read the handler diff (`api/routes.py:8292-8358`), the canonical pattern it mirrors, `_profiles_match` (`api/profiles.py:251-275`), and all four new tests. This is a clean, correct security fix — and I verified two things the description and greptile didn't explicitly cover.

## The pattern is an exact match for the proven one

The new scoping block is byte-for-byte the same shape as the already-shipped list-sessions handler:

```python
# api/routes.py:5494-5503 (existing, list-sessions)
active_profile = get_active_profile_name()
all_profiles = _all_profiles_query_flag(parsed)
...
if _profiles_match(s.get("profile"), active_profile)
```

and `_profiles_match` correctly treats `None`/`''`/`'default'` and a renamed-root display name as equivalent (`profiles.py:268-273`), so legacy rows tagged `default` and renamed-root rows both stay visible to the right profile and invisible to others. Filtering `sessions` once at line 8295 and iterating that filtered list in both the empty-query branch (8313) and the search loop (8323) means the `get_session()` content-scan at line 8334 can never be reached for an other-profile ID. That's the important part — the disclosure wasn't just titles, it was transcript bodies via content search, and the single up-front filter closes both.

## The content-search test is not vacuous (worth noting since `depth=0` looks suspicious)

`test_content_search_should_not_return_other_profile_rows` uses `depth=0`, which at first glance looks like it would skip message scanning entirely. It doesn't — the slice logic is:

```python
msgs = sess.messages[:depth] if depth else sess.messages
```

`depth=0` is falsy, so it scans the **full** message list. So the "secret needle body" in `other-content-s` genuinely gets scanned, and only `_profiles_match` keeps it out of results. That makes it a real adversarial test of the leak path, not a no-op. Good.

## I checked the sibling `all_sessions()` call sites — search was the last unscoped disclosure surface

There are four other `all_sessions()` consumers in `routes.py`; none is a comparable leak:

- `:4332` — deep-health check, returns only `len(sessions)` (a count), no per-row metadata.
- `:5378` region — inside the list-sessions handler that already applies `_profiles_match` at 5494.
- `:7533` — pin-quota counting (`_session_counts_toward_pin_quota`), aggregate by design.

So `/api/sessions/search` really was the one remaining endpoint querying `all_sessions()` raw and returning user-facing rows. After this PR the profile-isolation model is consistent across the session/project read surface.

## One low-priority follow-up (out of scope here)

`:7533` counts pins toward the 3-pin quota across *all* profiles (it snapshots `all_sessions()` without `_profiles_match`). That's not an information disclosure — it returns no other-profile data to the client — but it does mean pins in profile B can consume profile A's quota. Probably intentional (a global pin cap), but if pins are meant to be per-profile it'd be a separate small fix. Flagging only so it's a conscious decision, not for this PR.

The unrelated `test_profile_skills_stats` failure you noted does reproduce on master, so it's correctly out of scope. LGTM.

pull_list.title: fix(tests): tree-kill ctl.sh stop on Windows (#3669)
pull_list.body:
## Thinking Path

- `ctl.sh stop` only signaled the recorded parent PID, but the Windows/Git Bash test launcher runs as a bash process with looping `sleep` children.
- The test cleanup helper already knows how to kill a process tree on Windows, but `assert_process_exits` returns as soon as the parent disappears, so child cleanup can be skipped.
- The fix makes `ctl.sh stop` tree-kill through `taskkill` on Windows while preserving POSIX signal behavior, then hardens test cleanup so fake bash launchers do not leave descendants behind.

## What Changed

- `ctl.sh`: route Windows/Git Bash stop and force-stop paths through `taskkill //F //T` after translating the recorded Git Bash PID to its Windows PID, while keeping POSIX `kill` and `kill -KILL` behavior unchanged.
- `ctl.sh`: make the ownership guard understand Git Bash process tables that lack `ps -o args=`, and compare both Windows and Git Bash path spellings before treating a PID as owned by WebUI.
- `tests/test_ctl_script.py`: call `_kill_tree(pid)` after successful stop cleanup in the three fake Python tests, map PID namespaces in the Windows cleanup helpers, and use `_kill_tree(started_pid)` in the alternate-port cleanup path.
- `tests/test_ctl_script.py`: wait for complete fake-python log lines and normalize mixed Windows/Git Bash path separators so the Windows ctl regression test validates the process cleanup instead of failing early on harness assumptions.

## Why It Matters

Windows test runs should not leak bash/sleep child processes after `ctl.sh stop` removes the recorded parent PID. Keeping the POSIX path unchanged limits the behavioral change to the platform that needs process-tree cleanup.

## Verification

```powershell
$env:PYTHONUTF8 = '1'
..\hermes-agent\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest tests/test_ctl_script.py -v --timeout=60
..\hermes-agent\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest tests/ -v --timeout=60
```

Targeted result: `tests/test_ctl_script.py` passes locally on Windows with 7 passed, 1 skipped. Full-suite result: attempted locally on Windows, but the shared test fixture stops during setup at `tests/test_issue1633_models_cache_version_stamp.py::test_save_overwrite_atomic` with `PermissionError: [WinError 5] Access is denied` while deleting a generated `.git/objects` file under `C:\Apps\hermes\webui-test-*`; this is outside the ctl.sh change.

## Risks / Follow-ups

- The Windows branch depends on `taskkill` and Git Bash process table PID mapping being available; it falls back to the existing signal behavior if the Windows PID cannot be resolved.
- `taskkill //F` is forceful even for the initial stop, but `taskkill` without `/F` timed out against the fake Git Bash process locally, and the branch is scoped away from POSIX hosts.
- `wmic` is used only as a Windows command-line fallback when Git Bash `ps` cannot provide args; if it is absent, the guard falls back to `ps -f` and otherwise refuses to treat the PID as owned.

## Model Used

GPT-5.5 via Codex CLI

issue_list.title: bug(terminal): embedded /terminal silently fails for non-local terminal backends (ssh/docker) — workspace layer is remote-aware (#3486) but the PTY spawn layer is not
issue_list.body:
## Summary

The embedded `/terminal` (composer terminal panel) is a **local-PTY-only** feature. When a
profile is configured with a **non-local terminal backend** (`terminal.backend` = `ssh`,
`docker`, etc. in the agent's `config.yaml`), `/terminal` cannot work, and the failure is
opaque to the user — it reads as "doesn't do anything."

Reported in Discord #webui:

> **@Pinched-Nerve** (2026-06-05): "/terminal — nope, doesn't do anything. I wonder… if the
> profile is set up to use a non-local workspace (such as docker or ssh), does '/terminal'
> still work?"

The reporter's hypothesis is correct: it does **not** work for a non-local backend, and the
reason is an architectural split between two layers.

## Root cause — workspace layer is remote-aware, spawn layer is not

WebUI gained partial remote-terminal-backend awareness in **#3486 / v0.51.234**
("Remote/SSH terminal profiles can now use target-side workspace paths that don't exist on
the WebUI host"). That change lives entirely in the **workspace validation/resolution**
layer:

- `api/workspace.py:60` `_is_remote_terminal_backend(cfg)` → `True` when
  `terminal.backend` ∉ `{'', 'local'}`.
- `api/workspace.py:68` `_remote_terminal_cwd()` + `_remote_terminal_workspace_candidate()`
  → allow paths under `terminal.cwd` to resolve **without a server-local `stat()`**.
- `resolve_trusted_workspace()` therefore now **accepts** a target-side path that doesn't
  exist on the WebUI host.

But the actual **terminal spawn** layer was never updated. `api/terminal.py` has **zero**
references to `backend` / `remote` / `ssh` / `docker`. `start_terminal()`
(`api/terminal.py:268`) does two host-local things unconditionally:

```python
cwd = str(Path(workspace).expanduser().resolve())
if not Path(cwd).is_dir():
    raise ValueError("workspace is not a directory")   # line 276
...
master_fd, slave_fd = os.openpty()                     # always a LOCAL pty
shell = _shell_path()                                  # always the WebUI host's shell
```

So for a non-local backend there are two failure modes:

1. **Remote-only workspace path** (the common case — `terminal.cwd` lives on the target, not
   the WebUI host): `resolve_trusted_workspace()` lets the path through (#3486), then
   `start_terminal()` re-runs `is_dir()` against the local FS → `ValueError("workspace is
   not a directory")` → `/api/terminal/start` returns 400 → the client surfaces a brief
   `terminal_start_failed` toast and the panel closes. Net effect: "does nothing."
2. **Path that happens to exist locally too**: `start_terminal()` succeeds but opens a shell
   on the **WebUI host**, not the docker/ssh target the agent actually runs commands in —
   silently wrong environment.

Verified locally:

```
>>> from api.terminal import start_terminal
>>> start_terminal('s', '/workspace')   # docker-style target path
ValueError: workspace is not a directory
```

## Two distinct things here

- **(A) Confirmed architectural gap (this issue):** the embedded terminal does not support
  non-local terminal backends, and the half-supported state introduced by #3486 (workspace
  layer accepts remote paths, spawn layer rejects them / runs locally) makes it fail
  confusingly instead of degrading gracefully.
- **(B) Reporter's specific "does nothing":** could be (A), **or** simply the
  no-workspace-selected path — `cmdTerminal()` (`static/commands.js:584`) shows a
  `terminal_no_workspace_title` ("Select a workspace to open terminal") warning toast and
  returns when the session has no workspace. That toast is brief and easy to miss → also
  reads as "nothing happened." To confirm which path @Pinched-Nerve hit we'd want: their
  `terminal.backend` value, whether a workspace was selected, and what (if any) toast
  appeared. (A) is file-worthy regardless.

## Suggested fix / fix shape

Make the spawn layer backend-aware so the two layers agree. Options:

- **Minimum (graceful failure):** in `start_terminal()` / `_handle_terminal_start`, detect
  `_is_remote_terminal_backend()` and, instead of the generic `is_dir()` `ValueError`,
  return a clear, actionable error ("Embedded terminal is not available for ssh/docker
  terminal backends" — analogous to the existing Windows `NotImplementedError`). Also gate
  the `/terminal` command / terminal button so it doesn't appear actionable when the backend
  is non-local. This removes the silent/misleading failure even if full support is deferred.
- **Full support (larger):** route the PTY through the configured backend — spawn
  `ssh <host>` / `docker exec -it <container>` as the shell (using `terminal.backend` +
  connection settings) instead of the local `_shell_path()`, with `cwd` applied target-side.
  This is the "does `/terminal` actually work over ssh/docker" answer the reporter is asking
  for. Bigger scope; touches `_shell_argv`/`_shell_path` and the spawn request in
  `api/terminal.py`, plus connection config plumbing.

Recommend shipping the **minimum graceful-failure** path first (kills the confusing
"does nothing"), then tracking full remote-PTY support as the larger enhancement.

## Scope

- Layer: WebUI server (`api/terminal.py`, `api/routes.py:_handle_terminal_start`) +
  small client gating (`static/commands.js` `cmdTerminal`, terminal button sync in
  `static/terminal.js`). Possibly a new i18n key for the clearer error.
- Related prior work: #3486 / v0.51.234 (workspace layer remote-awareness) — this issue is
  the un-finished spawn-layer half of that.

## Reported by

@Pinched-Nerve in Discord **#webui** (2026-06-05).

events.body:
> @Pinched-Nerve in Discord #webui (2026-06-05).

I know that guy.  He's a real whack job.

Read `api/terminal.py`, `api/workspace.py`, `api/routes.py`, and `static/commands.js` on `origin/master`. The diagnosis in this issue is correct — the workspace layer and the spawn layer genuinely disagree, and I can confirm the exact 400 path.

## Code reference — the two layers disagree

Workspace resolution **bypasses** the local `is_dir()` for remote backends (`api/workspace.py:120-133`):

```python
remote_terminal = _is_remote_terminal_backend(terminal_cfg)
...
if cwd and str(cwd) not in ('.', ''):
    p = Path(str(cwd)).expanduser().resolve()
    if remote_terminal or p.is_dir():   # remote_terminal short-circuits the stat
        return str(p)
```

But the spawn layer re-applies it unconditionally (`api/terminal.py:275-276`):

```python
cwd = str(Path(workspace).expanduser().resolve())
if not Path(cwd).is_dir():
    raise ValueError("workspace is not a directory")
```

`api/terminal.py` has zero references to `backend`/`remote`/`ssh`/`docker` — `grep -n "backend\|remote\|ssh\|docker" api/terminal.py` returns nothing. So for a target-side `terminal.cwd` that doesn't exist on the WebUI host, `resolve_trusted_workspace()` (workspace.py) lets it through, then `start_terminal()` (terminal.py:276) rejects it.

## How it surfaces as "does nothing"

The route maps that `ValueError` straight to HTTP 400 (`api/routes.py:8642-8643`):

```python
except ValueError as e:
    return bad(handler, str(e), 400)
```

`_handle_terminal_start` (routes.py:8621) calls `start_terminal` with no backend check, so the client gets a 400 and shows the brief `terminal_start_failed` toast, then the panel closes — the reported "nope, doesn't do anything." And note the second failure mode is real too: if the path *happens* to exist locally, `os.openpty()` + `_shell_path()` (terminal.py:287, 306) open a shell on the **WebUI host**, not the docker/ssh target — silently wrong environment.

## On the reporter's specific case

The issue already flags the ambiguity, and it's worth keeping: `cmdTerminal()` also bails when no workspace is selected (`static/commands.js:586-589`):

```js
if(!S.session||!S.session.workspace){
  showToast(t('terminal_no_workspace_title'),2600,'warning');
  ...
  return;
}
```

That toast is equally easy to miss, so "does nothing" could be either path. But the architectural gap (A) is file-worthy on its own regardless of which one Pinched-Nerve hit.

## Recommendation

The minimum graceful-failure fix is the right first ship and it's small: in `start_terminal()` (or earlier, in `_handle_terminal_start`), detect the remote backend before the `is_dir()` check and raise a clear, actionable error — mirroring the existing Windows guard at `api/terminal.py:270-271` (`NotImplementedError("Embedded terminal is not supported on Windows")`). Concretely:

```python
# api/terminal.py, top of start_terminal(), after the _TERMINAL_SUPPORTED guard
from api.workspace import _is_remote_terminal_backend
from api.config import get_config
if _is_remote_terminal_backend(get_config().get('terminal', {})):
    raise NotImplementedError(
        "Embedded terminal is not available for ssh/docker terminal backends")
```

Then map `NotImplementedError` to a 501 (or a dedicated 4xx) in `_handle_terminal_start` and gate the `/terminal` command + terminal button in `static/commands.js`/`static/terminal.js` so it doesn't look actionable when the backend is non-local. That kills the misleading silent failure even if full remote-PTY support is deferred.

## Cross-repo note for full support (larger)

The agent already defines these backends — `local/docker/modal/ssh/daytona` (`hermes_cli/setup.py:1154` agent-side) — and is fully backend-aware in its own command execution and prompt building (`agent/prompt_builder.py:188`, `agent/file_safety.py:459`). Full support means the WebUI spawn layer routing the PTY through the configured backend (e.g. `docker exec -it <container>` / `ssh <host>` as the shell argv instead of `_shell_path()`), reusing the agent's connection config rather than re-deriving it. That's the bigger enhancement; the graceful-failure path should land first.

issue_list.title: bug(models): picked model reverts to previous/default model on send (likely #3448 profile-aware resolution, v0.51.290)
issue_list.body:
# bug(models): picked model reverts to the previous/default model on send (likely #3448 profile-aware resolution, v0.51.290)

## Summary

A user changes the model in the composer picker, sends a message, and the picker **snaps back to the previously-used model** instead of running the model they just selected. Reported in Discord #webui (2026-06-06).

> getting an issue where i change the model but when i send a message it reverts back to the latest model that was used
> — @123321

## What happens (client → server → client trace)

1. **Picker change** persists fine. `$('modelSelect').onchange` (`static/boot.js:1176`) sets `S.session.model`, writes the persisted model state, and POSTs `/api/session/update`. The dropdown shows the new model.
2. **On send**, the client sends the picked model to `/api/chat/start` (`static/messages.js:657-666`):
   ```js
   const _modelState=_chatPayloadModelState();   // model: S.session.model || modelSelect.value
   await api('/api/chat/start',{method:'POST',body:JSON.stringify({
     ..., model:_modelState.model, model_provider:_modelState.model_provider, ...
   })});
   ```
3. **Server resolves** the model (`api/routes.py:11301-11314`):
   ```py
   requested_model = body.get("model") or s.model
   requested_provider = body.get("model_provider") if "model_provider" in body else getattr(s, "model_provider", None)
   _pp_provider, _pp_default = _read_profile_model_config(s, requested_provider)
   model, model_provider, normalized_model = _resolve_compatible_session_model_state(
       requested_model, requested_provider,
       profile_provider=_pp_provider, profile_default_model=_pp_default,
   )
   ```
   When `normalized_model` is true, the handler returns the rewritten model as `effective_model` (`api/routes.py:11053-11054`).
4. **Client echoes it back into the picker** (`static/messages.js:670-675`):
   ```js
   if(startData.effective_model && S.session){
     S.session.model=startData.effective_model;
     ...
     if($('modelSelect')) _applyModelToDropdown(startData.effective_model, $('modelSelect'), ...);
   }
   ```
   → the just-picked model is overwritten in the dropdown. **This is the visible revert.**

## Leading root cause: profile-aware normalization (new in v0.51.290 / #3448)

`_resolve_compatible_session_model_state` gained a **profile-aware** branch in **#3448** (shipped **v0.51.290**, Release JF / stage-s1, commit `47020925`, 2026-06-04, "fixes #3405"). When the session is bound to a profile and the picked model is sent **without** an explicit `model_provider` / `@provider:` qualifier, the resolver compares the picked model's family against the profile's configured provider and, on a mismatch, **rewrites it to the profile default** (`api/routes.py:2005-2044`):

```py
model_family = ""   # gpt / claude / gemini prefix of the picked model
...
if model_family and model_family != _profile_provider_normalized:
    _target = _profile_default or default_model
    return _target, profile_provider, True          # ← normalized_model=True, model swapped
...
if "/" in model and model_provider_from_name and model_provider_from_name != _profile_provider_normalized:
    _target = _profile_default or default_model
    return _target, profile_provider, True
```

So if the user picks a model whose family doesn't match the profile's provider (e.g. a `gpt-*` pick under a profile whose `model.provider` is `anthropic`), and the picker option didn't carry an explicit provider, the server swaps it for the profile default — i.e. "the latest model that was used" — and the client snaps the dropdown back. `_read_profile_model_config` only short-circuits (returns `None,None`, disabling profile normalization) when an explicit `requested_provider` is present, so this only bites picks sent **without** a provider context.

This is the **visible-revert** counterpart to #3405 (which was *invisible* provider divergence — pill showed one model, ran another). #3448 was meant to make the profile authoritative; the side effect is that a deliberate cross-family pick gets treated as a stale-session artifact and repaired away.

## Secondary factor (independent of the cause above)

Even when normalization is "correct," the client applies `effective_model` to the picker **unconditionally** (`messages.js:675`). If the server ever returns an `effective_model` that differs from the user's deliberate pick, the UI silently discards the selection with no toast/explanation — the user just sees it flip back. A deliberate user pick arguably shouldn't be overridden, or if it must be, the UI should say why (mismatch warning), not silently revert.

## Steps to reproduce (hypothesis — needs reporter confirmation)

1. Run a session under a **profile** whose `model.provider` is set (e.g. `anthropic`).
2. In the composer model picker, select a model from a **different family** that has no explicit provider qualifier (e.g. a bare `gpt-*` entry).
3. Send a message.
4. **Observe:** the picker reverts to the profile's default / previously-used model, and the turn runs on that model rather than the pick.

## Need-info (to pin the exact path)

The report is brief (no version/provider/model). To confirm whether this is the #3448 profile path or a different normalization branch, please ask the reporter for:
- WebUI version (`Settings → About`) — confirm it's ≥ **v0.51.290** (when #3448 landed).
- Whether they're on a **custom profile** (and its `model.provider`) or the default profile.
- The exact **from → to** models (what they picked vs. what it reverted to).
- The provider the picked model belongs to.

## Suggested fix shape

- Treat an **explicit composer pick** as authoritative: when the model came from a deliberate picker selection (not a stale persisted session model), the profile-aware repair in `_resolve_compatible_session_model_state` should **not** rewrite it to the profile default. Distinguish "stale session model needs repair" from "user just chose this model" — e.g. pass a flag from the chat-start payload indicating the model was explicitly selected this turn, and skip the family-mismatch rewrite in that case.
- Alternatively/additionally: when the picked option lacks a provider context, resolve+attach the picked model's own provider rather than swapping the model, so the family mismatch is reconciled by routing, not by changing the model.
- Client: don't silently `_applyModelToDropdown(effective_model)` over a deliberate pick — if the server normalizes a user's explicit selection, surface a toast ("model X isn't available under profile Y's provider; using Z") instead of a silent revert.
- Regression test: a chat-start with an explicit cross-family model pick under a provider-bound profile asserts the response `effective_model` equals the pick (or that a mismatch is surfaced, not silently swapped).

## Scope

`api/routes.py` (`_resolve_compatible_session_model_state` profile-aware branch + `_handle_chat_start` plumbing of an "explicit pick" signal) and `static/messages.js` (the `effective_model` echo at 670-675). Backend-led.

## Related

- #3448 — "respect profile provider in session model resolution" (shipped v0.51.290, the likely source of the new normalization). 
- #3405 — invisible profile/provider divergence (the issue #3448 fixed); this report is the visible-revert side effect of that fix.

## Reported by

@123321 in Discord #webui (2026-06-06). Root-cause trace agent-investigated; the #3448/v0.51.290 attribution is a strong hypothesis pending the reporter's version + profile/provider details.

pull_list.title: feat(sidebar): add manual session status labels (todo/in-progress/done) (#3199)
pull_list.body:
## Thinking Path

- The WebUI auto-derives session "needs attention" from agent activity, but users triaging multiple concurrent sessions have no way to track their own workflow state per session.
- A server-side status field would require a SessionDB schema migration and coordination with the gateway SSE watcher path; localStorage keyed to `session_id` delivers the same result with zero backend changes.
- The existing pattern for per-session localStorage maps (e.g., `hermes-session-viewed-counts` at sessions.js:158, `hermes-session-completion-unread` at sessions.js:159) is already established; this PR adds a fourth map `hermes-session-manual-status`.
- The session row builder at sessions.js:4433-4483 already appends pin, worktree, branch, and project-dot indicators inline in `titleRow`. A `session-manual-status` badge fits the same slot.
- The three-dot action menu at sessions.js:2395-2566 provides the primary interaction surface; badge click-to-cycle adds a secondary shortcut.
- Three status values (todo, in-progress, done) match the established `kanban_status_todo` vocabulary in i18n.js:666 and keep the option set minimal.

## What Changed

- `static/sessions.js`: add `SESSION_MANUAL_STATUS_KEY` constant; add `_getSessionManualStatuses()`, `getSessionManualStatus()`, `setSessionManualStatus()`, and `_cycleSessionManualStatus()` helpers; inject status badge into session row title row when a status is set; add three status-picker entries to the three-dot action menu before `_mountSessionActionMenu`.
- `static/style.css`: add `.session-manual-status` base rule and three status-specific color variants after `.session-project-dot`.
- `static/i18n.js`: add `session_status_todo`, `session_status_in_progress`, `session_status_done`, and `session_status_click_to_change` keys.

## Why It Matters

Users with multiple concurrent sessions can now mark each one Todo, In Progress, or Done directly from the sidebar, without renaming or relying on the auto-derived attention state. The badge persists across page reloads via localStorage and requires zero backend changes.

## Verification

```
# Full suite
pytest tests/ -v --timeout=60

# Manual: open WebUI, right-click a session, set a status, verify badge appears
# Reload page, confirm badge still present
# Click badge, confirm cycle: Todo → In Progress → Done → cleared
```

## Risks / Follow-ups

- localStorage is per-browser, not synced across devices. A follow-up API endpoint could persist status server-side.
- Stale localStorage entries for deleted sessions accumulate silently. A prune pass keyed to `_allSessions` during render would fix this; deferred to follow-up.
- No competing PR on this axis as of 2026-06-04.

## Model Used

Claude Opus 4.8 via Claude Code CLI

Closes #3199

pull_list.title: fix(terminal): guard embedded terminal on remote backends (#3673)
pull_list.body:
## Thinking Path

- The remote-workspace path handling already exists in `api/workspace.py`, but `/api/terminal/start` still funnels those paths into the local PTY spawn path.
- That means ssh/docker terminal backends fail late and opaquely in `start_terminal()` instead of being rejected deliberately at the route boundary.
- The smallest upstreamable fix is to add a backend guard in the route and surface the same state early in `/terminal` slash-command UX.

## What Changed

- `api/routes.py`: expose a remote-backend flag in `/api/workspaces` and reject `/api/terminal/start` for non-local backends with a stable error payload
- `static/commands.js`: preflight the new flag so `/terminal` stops before trying to open the embedded panel on remote backends
- `tests/test_embedded_workspace_terminal.py`: lock the backend guard and slash-command preflight into regression coverage

## Why It Matters

Users on ssh/docker profiles currently see a misleading terminal-start failure even though the real limitation is that the embedded PTY only supports local backends. This makes the limitation explicit and prevents the UI from advertising a broken path.

## Verification

```bash
pytest tests/test_embedded_workspace_terminal.py -v --timeout=60
pytest tests/ -v --timeout=60
```

## Risks / Follow-ups

- This does not add embedded remote-terminal support; it only makes the current local-only contract explicit and non-confusing.

## Model Used

OpenAI GPT-5 Codex

The change prevents the misleading late failure users on SSH/Docker backends previously experienced. - **`api/routes.py`**: imports `_is_remote_terminal_backend`, adds `terminal_remote_backend` to the workspaces payload, and adds a guard in `_handle_terminal_start` that returns a stable `remote_terminal_backend_unsupported` 400 before local PTY setup runs (though session lookup still executes first, as noted in a prior thread). - **`static/terminal.js` + `static/commands.js` + `static/panels.js`**: `syncTerminalBackendState` syncs `S.terminalRemoteBackend` from the workspaces response; `cmdTerminal` preflights the flag and exits early; `syncTerminalButton` disables the toggle and updates its tooltip for remote backends; `_startComposerTerminal` gains a `S.terminalRemoteBackend` guard — but it returns rather than throws, leaving the panel open when the guard fires mid-open. - **`static/i18n.js` + `tests/`**: adds `terminal_remote_backend_unsupported` to all 10 locales and locks the new behaviour into regression tests.

pull_list.title: [security] reject blocked roots for remote workspaces
pull_list.body:
## Summary

This hardens remote-terminal workspace resolution so the remote-workspace shortcut cannot accept blocked local system roots such as `/etc` when the configured remote terminal cwd is also under that root.

The normal local workspace path already rejects these roots, but `_remote_terminal_workspace_candidate()` returned early for paths under the remote cwd before the blocked-root guard ran. Later workspace file operations use `s.workspace` as a local `Path`, so accepting a remote cwd like `/etc` can convert the intended remote-side path into a trusted local workspace root.

## Security impact

Before this change, with an SSH/remote terminal profile whose target-side cwd is `/etc`, workspace resolution accepted `/etc` as `/private/etc` on macOS. A session created with that workspace could then pass the workspace to local file helpers, allowing reads from local system files such as `hosts` through workspace file-read paths.

Redacted local proof before the fix:

```text
remote_terminal_backend=ssh
remote_terminal_cwd=/etc
accepted_workspace=/private/etc
session_workspace=/private/etc
file_read_path=hosts
file_read_size=213
file_read_contains_localhost=True
file_read_first_line=##
```

After the fix, both registration and trusted workspace resolution reject the same root:

```text
validate_workspace_to_add=REJECTED ValueError: Path points to a system directory: /private/etc
resolve_trusted_workspace=REJECTED ValueError: Path points to a system directory: /private/etc
```

## Fix

- Apply the existing `_is_blocked_workspace_path()` guard inside `_remote_terminal_workspace_candidate()` before accepting candidate paths under the remote cwd.
- Check both the requested candidate and the configured remote cwd/base path.
- Add regression coverage for an SSH backend configured with `/etc` as cwd.

## Validation

```text
python3 -m pytest tests/test_remote_terminal_workspace.py tests/test_workspace_blocked_roots_macos.py tests/test_workspace_inaccessible_paths.py -q
41 passed, 1 warning in 2.09s
```

```text
python3 -m pytest tests/test_remote_terminal_workspace.py tests/test_workspace_blocked_roots_macos.py tests/test_workspace_inaccessible_paths.py tests/test_workspace_symlink_containment.py tests/test_workspace_upload.py tests/test_workspace_git.py -q
108 passed, 1 skipped, 1 warning in 12.97s
```

## Duplicate check

I checked public issue/PR searches for remote terminal workspace/system-root wording and did not find an exact duplicate. The closest visible issue was #3673, but that appears to cover terminal backend behavior rather than this blocked-root workspace/file-boundary case.

events.body:
Greptile Summary

 This PR hardens remote-workspace resolution by inserting `_is_blocked_workspace_path()` checks inside `_remote_terminal_workspace_candidate()` before the early-return that previously allowed blocked roots (e.g. `/etc`) to be accepted as valid remote workspaces. The fix correctly closes the explicit registration and resolution paths (`validate_workspace_to_add`, `resolve_trusted_workspace`). - The two-line guard in `api/workspace.py` checks both the requested candidate and the configured `terminal.cwd`, returning `None` for any blocked path so callers fall through to the existing `_is_blocked_workspace_path` raise. - The new parametrized test covers both the exact blocked root (`/etc`) and a sub-path (`/etc/ssh`) against both public validation functions. - `_profile_default_workspace()` still returns `terminal.cwd` (e.g. `/private/etc`) without a blocked-root check; after this fix `get_last_workspace()` always falls back to it for blocked-cwd profiles, flowing an unguarded system root into the media-serving `allowed_roots` calculation and crashing the session workspace recovery helper.

Confidence Score: 4/5

The explicit workspace validation functions (`validate_workspace_to_add`, `resolve_trusted_workspace`) are correctly hardened. However, `_profile_default_workspace()` returns `terminal.cwd` without a blocked-root check, and after this fix `get_last_workspace()` will consistently return that unguarded value for profiles with a blocked cwd — feeding it into the media-serving `allowed_roots` list and causing the workspace recovery helper to raise an exception rather than fall back gracefully. `api/workspace.py` — specifically the `_profile_default_workspace()` function and how its return value flows through `get_last_workspace()` into `routes.py`.

Important Files Changed

 | Filename | Overview | |----------|----------| | api/workspace.py | Adds blocked-root guard inside `_remote_terminal_workspace_candidate()` before the `_is_within` early-return; fix is correct for the explicit registration/resolution paths but `_profile_default_workspace()` still returns blocked cwd values without validation. | | tests/test_remote_terminal_workspace.py | Adds parametrized regression test covering both the exact blocked root (`/etc`) and a sub-path (`/etc/ssh`); tests both `validate_workspace_to_add` and `resolve_trusted_workspace`. |

Flowchart

 ```mermaid %%{init: {'theme': 'neutral'}}%% flowchart TD A["validate_workspace_to_add(path)\nor resolve_trusted_workspace(path)"] --> B["_remote_terminal_workspace_candidate(path)"] B --> C{"remote cwd\nconfigured?"} C -- No --> D["return None"] C -- Yes --> E["resolve candidate & base"] E --> F{"NEW: _is_blocked_workspace_path\n(candidate) OR (base)?"} F -- Yes --> G["return None ✅ (fix)"] F -- No --> H{"candidate == base\nor _is_within(base)?"} H -- No --> I["return None"] H -- Yes --> J["return candidate"] G --> K["Caller falls through to\n_is_blocked_workspace_path check"] K --> L["ValueError: Path points to\na system directory ✅"] M["get_last_workspace()"] --> N["valid_last_workspace(stored_path)"] N --> B2["_remote_terminal_workspace_candidate(stored_path)"] B2 --> O{"blocked cwd?"} O -- Yes --> P["return None (after fix)"] P --> Q["valid_last_workspace returns None"] Q --> R["_profile_default_workspace()"] R --> S["returns terminal.cwd resolved\n⚠️ no blocked-root check"] S --> T["get_last_workspace returns /private/etc"] T --> U["media handler: allowed_roots += /private/etc ⚠️"] T --> V["resolve_trusted_workspace raises ValueError — recovery broken ⚠️"] ```

 1. `api/workspace.py`, line 103-144 ([link](https://github.com/nesquena/hermes-webui/blob/184892b0bcfc63e54f481e85a45f3babfbff60d8/api/workspace.py#L103-L144)) **`_profile_default_workspace()` returns a blocked system root without validation** `_profile_default_workspace()` returns `terminal.cwd` resolved — `/private/etc` on macOS — without ever calling `_is_blocked_workspace_path`. This becomes a problem because this fix (correctly) makes `_remote_terminal_workspace_candidate()` return `None` for every path under a blocked cwd, which causes `get_last_workspace()` to **always** fall back to `_profile_default_workspace()` for these profiles. That fallback value is then used in two places without a blocked-root guard: 1. `_resolve_chat_workspace_with_recovery` (line 11391) calls `resolve_trusted_workspace(get_last_workspace())` as a recovery fallback.
